title: Product photography for a skincare brand
excerpt: Photograph the bottle and the texture under one light, and keep claims in the text. Mixed crops make a quiet line look unfinished.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. Skincare photography is a controlled setup: one light, one crop, claims left out of the frame.
caption: Work by a window, one setup, claims left in the text. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the minimum photo set for a skincare product?
faqs.answer: The container on the shared background, with the label matching what you ship, and a texture frame of the cream, oil, or gel. A second angle is useful when the pump or cap is how people use it. Faces and medical props are optional at best, and most small brands should skip them.

faqs.question: Can claims live in the photograph?
faqs.answer: They should not. Badges and percentages painted into the file go stale and are a poor text alternative. Describe the bottle in the alt text, and put ingredients and use in the page. When the formula's color changes, reshoot the texture so the picture and the list stay the same product.

faqs.question: How do you stop a serum line from looking unfinished?
faqs.answer: One background, one camera height per format, and the same margin so a sample looks smaller than a full bottle. Shoot shades of one product in a single row of light. A cheek, a marble slab, and a blue gel as three thumbnails will undo a quiet brand.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A skincare brand product photography practice should show the product and the texture, with restraint, under one crop and one light. Ingredients and claims belong in text, not in badges burned into the picture. Mixed crops and mixed marble backgrounds make a small line look unfinished, and they make quiet formulas look like they are shouting.

Photograph the container you ship and the texture of what is inside. Stop when those two are clear. A wall of claims is a copy problem that photography should refuse to illustrate.

## The bottle, the texture, and nothing extra

Each product needs a short set.

- A hero of the container, label readable, on the shared background, cropped like the rest of the line.
- A second angle if the cap, the pump, or the shape is how people use it.
- A texture frame: the cream, oil, or gel on a surface that does not recolor it, in the same light.
- A use frame only if application is the question, and then with the same restraint as the hero. No bathroom opera.

The label in the hero should match the label you are shipping, including the size. A 50 milliliter bottle photographed as if it were the 100 is a fact error. When you change the label, you change the file before the new batch is on the site. An old claim on a new label, still living in the hero, will outrun the careful sentences on the page.

Do not set claims in the image. "Dermatologist approved," "72-hour," and star ratings painted on the JPEG cannot be updated, translated, or read reliably as text. The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) asks for a text alternative that describes the picture, and for information to exist as text. Alt can be "Frosted glass bottle with a white pump, front label, on a pale grey background." The ingredient list and the how-to live on the page. The W3C principles include perceivable and understandable. A claim that exists only inside a picture fails both when the picture is the only place it appears.

## Light, color, and texture that stay honest

Choose a light and keep it. Soft, from one side, quiet enough that a white bottle does not clip and a brown glass bottle does not turn black. Shoot the line together. Serums photographed months apart under warmer and colder light will look like they come from different brands, and the grid will feel unfinished even if each frame is pretty.

Texture is where retouching goes too far. Show the cream as it sits. Do not paint it into a plastic swirl that the product cannot make. Buyers who open the jar will compare. A mismatch reads as a broken promise, which is a strange outcome for a brand that wanted to look premium. Gloss that is real can stay. Gloss that is drawn will not match the bottle shot beside it.

Color of the product and color of the formula are both promises. A tinted cream must look like the tint, not like a universal beige you liked on the monitor. Check the file next to the open jar, in daylight, on a phone. You will not calibrate every buyer's screen. You can catch a file that is a different product.

Glass and liquid need a background that does not rewrite the color. If the blue set turns a clear serum blue, the serum is no longer itself. Use the neutral ground you chose for the line, and let the liquid be the color it is. That is the restraint. A dramatic gel on a dramatic ground is a poster. The catalog needs a product.

## One background for the whole line

Pick one ground: a paper, a single stone, a painted board. Use it for every hero. Marble for the oil, tile for the cream, and a model's cheek for the balm is the mixed grid. The cheek can be a secondary frame on that product's page if you have a real reason and a consistent way to shoot skin. It should not be the only thumbnail, because then the category becomes a collage of faces and bottles and nobody can compare the line.

Keep the camera distance and height constant per format. Bottles share a height. Jars share a height. Tubes share a height. Fill the frame by the same margin so a small sample looks small and a large bottle looks large. Zooming the sample until it dominates is a scale lie, and skincare buyers use size as a price comparison.

Leave space for the label to remain readable when the template rounds a corner or adds a quiet caption. Test the hero in the real grid on a phone. If the product name on the label cannot be read, that is acceptable only because the page title carries the name in text. If neither is readable, the crop is wrong.

Reflections in a pump can be cleaned when they hide the label. They should not be wiped so thoroughly that the bottle looks like an illustration. The material is part of the trust. Plastic that is photographed as glass will feel like a lie in the hand.

## Speed and stability

The hero is often the largest element on the page, so it sets the loading and the stability. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) guidance asks for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Export the display size rather than a camera original. Reserve the ratio in the layout so the price and the ingredient list do not jump when the bottle arrives. A jump next to "subscribe" and "buy once" is how the wrong choice gets tapped.

Name files by product, size, and view. When a shade launches, the name should tell the uploader which frame is which. The wrong tint on the page is a photography handoff failure, and it is also a product failure, because the buyer will receive a different face of the cream than the one they chose.

Keep masters with the margin intact. The next crop of the template should not force you to chop the cap off. A direction page records the master, the export, and the alt pattern so a new photographer does not invent a closer crop because it looked stronger in isolation.

## What not to stage

Do not stage medical props: stethoscopes, latex gloves, fake lab glass. You are not a clinic, and the pictures should not borrow one. Do not stage fruit and leaves unless the ingredient is in the formula and you are willing for people to think the jar contains the fruit. A strawberry beside a product that contains a synthetic fragrance is a claim.

Do not use before-and-after as the hero of the catalog. If a single documented result belongs anywhere, it belongs deep on a page with the conditions written out, and many brands should leave it out. The thumbnail is the bottle. The category is a shelf, not a transformation ad.

Do not change the background for a holiday and only reshoot the promotion. The holiday frame can be a banner. The product grid stays the system. A half-seasonal shelf is the mixed-crop problem again, with tinsel.

Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a useful comparison for brands that need the pictures and the interface to share one quiet idea. Bring the grid on a phone. The review is whether any tile is louder than the formula.

## Skin in the frame, if you use it at all

A smear on a forearm can explain texture. It can also imply a result. If you include skin, keep the crop tight on the product and the texture, not on a face that reads as a transformation. Use the same lighting as the bottle so the two frames belong together. Do not grade the skin warmer than the product to look healthier. That grade is a quiet claim.

Consent and context matter. The person whose arm or face appears has agreed to this use, and the frame does not suggest a medical condition unless you are prepared to document it as carefully as any other claim. Most brands at this size should skip faces. A consistent smear on a neutral surface carries texture without borrowing a person.

If you skip skin entirely, the texture frame still has to show whether the product is a gel, a cream, or an oil. Buyers use that cue when the ingredient list is long. A bottle alone, repeated forty times, makes the line look like packaging with no substance. One honest texture per product is enough. It does not need a bathroom, a robe, or a window full of morning light that you cannot repeat for the next launch.

## Direction that survives a new shade

Write one page: background, height per format, the frame set, export size, alt pattern, and the rule that claims and ingredients stay in text. When you add a shade or a size, you follow the page. You do not art-direct a new personality for the darker tint because it "feels different." The formula's family is the point. The tint is a variant inside it.

On set, shoot all shades of one product in a row, same light, before you move the stand. Later is how the middle shade ends up warmer than its siblings. Rejects get a word: clipped label, wrong height, fruit, claim in frame. Next month you will not put the fruit back.

If the formula's color changes because the recipe changed, reshoot the texture frame. Keeping the old swirl with the new ingredient list splits the truth across the page. The photograph and the list have to be the same product. That is the whole restraint, applied to files.

A bookstore is a different object, already made of words. [An online shop for a bookstore](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-bookstore) is the next piece in this series, because the page has to sell a specific book rather than a jar, and the same refusal of a marketplace grid still applies.
